claim: Making optimal decisions in the face of noise requires balancing short-term speed and accuracy.
source: Making optimal decisions in the face of noise requires balancing short-term speed and accuracy.
evidence: This is a general statement about decision-making that draws from established understanding in the field.

claim: Short-term speed can influence long-term accuracy through learning.
source: But a theory of optimality should account for the fact that short-term speed can influence long-term accuracy through learning.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim that is supported by the subsequent experimental and modeling work in the manuscript.

claim: Long-term learning is an important dynamical dimension of the speed-accuracy trade-off.
source: Here, we demonstrate that long-term learning is an important dynamical dimension of the speed-accuracy trade-off.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and modeling.

claim: Choosing suboptimal response times to learn faster sacrifices immediate reward but can lead to greater total reward.
source: The model reveals that choosing suboptimal response times to learn faster sacrifices immediate reward, but can lead to greater total reward.
evidence: This is a finding from the theoretical model that is subsequently tested experimentally.

claim: There is a relationship between stimulus exposure and learning speed.
source: We empirically verify predictions of the theory, including a relationship between stimulus exposure and learning speed
evidence: This is an experimental finding that confirms a model prediction.

claim: Reaction time is modulated by future learning prospects.
source: and a modulation of reaction time by future learning prospects.
evidence: This is an experimental finding that confirms a model prediction.

claim: Rats' strategies approximately maximize total reward over the full learning epoch.
source: We find that rats' strategies approximately maximize total reward over the full learning epoch
evidence: This is a primary finding based on analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Rats exhibit cognitive control over the learning process.
source: suggesting cognitive control over the learning process.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: Optimal behavior in decision making is frequently defined as maximization of reward over time.
source: Optimal behavior in decision making is frequently defined as maximization of reward over time (Gold and Shadlen, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Maximizing reward over time requires balancing the speed and accuracy of one's choices.
source: and this requires balancing the speed and accuracy of one's choices (Bogacz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The ideal balance of speed and accuracy differs considerably in cases of high and low competence.
source: The ideal balance of speed and accuracy differs considerably in the cases of high and low competence.
evidence: This is illustrated through the quiz examples and is a logical inference from the speed-accuracy trade-off.

claim: Competence can change as a function of experience through learning.
source: However, there is an important additional dynamical aspect to consider: competence can change as a function of experience through learning.
evidence: This is a general statement about learning that is well-established.

claim: The drift-diffusion model is one of the most prolific decision making models.
source: Perceptual decisions, in particular two-choice decisions, allow us to leverage one of the most prolific decision making models, the drift-diffusion model (DDM) (Ratcliff, 1978)
evidence: This is supported by a citation and is a well-known fact in the field.

claim: The speed-accuracy trade-off is one of the most prolific paradigms captured by the drift-diffusion model.
source: and one of the most prolific paradigms captured by it, the speed-accuracy trade-off (SAT), as a measurement of optimal behavior (i.e. maximization of reward per unit time) (Woodworth, 1899, Henmon, 1911, Garrett, 1922, Pew, 1969, Pachella, 1974, Wickelgren, 1977, Ruthruff, 1996, Ratcliff and Rouder, 1998, Gold and Shadlen, 2002, Bogacz et al., 2006; Bogacz et al., 2010; Heitz and Schall, 2012; Heitz, 2014, Rahnev and Denison, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Studies of the SAT have focused on how the brain may solve it.
source: Studies of the SAT have focused on how the brain may solve it (Gold and Shadlen, 2002, Roitman and Shadlen, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Studies of the SAT have focused on what the optimal solution is.
source: what the optimal solution is (Bogacz et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Studies of the SAT have focused on whether agents can manage it.
source: and whether agents can indeed manage it (Simen et al., 2006, Balci et al., 2011a; Simen et al., 2009; Bogacz et al., 2010, Drugowitsch et al., 2014, Drugowitsch et al., 2015; Manohar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Several studies have established the presence of a SAT in rodents.
source: Though most work in this area has taken place in humans and non-human primates, several studies have established the presence of a SAT in rodents (Uchida and Mainen, 2003, Abraham et al., 2004; Rinberg et al., 2006; Reinagel, 2013a; Reinagel, 2013b; Kurylo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: After extensive training, many subjects come close to optimal performance.
source: The broad conclusion of much of this literature is that after extensive training, many subjects come close to optimal performance (Simen et al., 2009Bogacz et al., 2010; Balci et al., 2011b; Zacksenhouse et al., 2010, Balci et al., 2011b, Starns and Ratcliff, 2010, Holmes and Cohen, 2014, Drugowitsch et al., 2014, Drugowitsch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Several hypotheses have been proposed for deviations from optimality, including error avoidance, poor internal estimates of time, and minimization of cognitive cost.
source: When faced with deviations from optimality, several hypotheses have been proposed, including error avoidance, poor internal estimates of time, and a minimization of the cognitive cost associated with an optimal strategy (Maddox and Bohil, 1998, Bogacz et al., 2006, Zacksenhouse et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Past studies have shown how agents behave after reaching steady-state performance.
source: Past studies have shown how agents behave after reaching steady-state performance (Simen et al., 2009, Starns and Ratcliff, 2010, Bogacz et al., 2010Zacksenhouse et al., 2010, Balci et al., 2011b, Balci et al., 2011a; Starns and Ratcliff, 2010, Drugowitsch et al., 2014, Drugowitsch et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Relatively less attention has been paid to how agents learn to approach near-optimal behavior.
source: but relatively less attention has been paid to how agents learn to approach near-optimal behavior (but see Law and Gold, 2009, Balci et al., 2011b, Drugowitsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the literature supported by citations.

claim: Maximizing instantaneous reward rate is a sensible goal when the task is fully mastered.
source: While maximizing instantaneous reward rate is a sensible goal when the task is fully mastered, it is less clear that this objective is appropriate during learning.
evidence: This is a logical inference about optimal strategies.

claim: It is less clear that maximizing instantaneous reward rate is appropriate during learning.
source: While maximizing instantaneous reward rate is a sensible goal when the task is fully mastered, it is less clear that this objective is appropriate during learning.
evidence: This is a logical inference that motivates the study.

claim: Fast responses mean minimal stimulus exposure, little opportunity for perceptual processing, and consequently slow learning.
source: However, fast responses mean minimal stimulus exposure, little opportunity for perceptual processing, and consequently slow learning.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between response time and learning.

claim: Response time and learning speed are causally related.
source: We then experimentally tested and confirmed several model predictions by evaluating whether response time and learning speed are causally related
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 5.

claim: Rats choose their response times to take advantage of learning opportunities.
source: and whether rats choose their response times so as to take advantage of learning opportunities.
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6.

claim: Rats adapt their behavior to approximately accrue maximal total reward across the entire learning trajectory.
source: Our results suggest that rats exhibit cognitive control of the learning process, adapting their behavior to approximately accrue maximal total reward across the entire learning trajectory
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: A policy that prioritizes learning in perceptual tasks may be advantageous from a total reward perspective.
source: and indicate that a policy that prioritizes learning in perceptual tasks may be advantageous from a total reward perspective.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Rats began a trial by licking the central of three capacitive lick ports.
source: The rats began a trial by licking the central of three capacitive lick ports, at which time a static visual object that varied in size and rotation from one of two categories appeared on a screen.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: When correct, rats received a water reward, and when incorrect, a timeout period.
source: When correct, they received a water reward, and when incorrect, a timeout period (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and is shown in figures.

claim: Ignored trials made up a small fraction of all trials.
source: Because this was a free-response task, rats were also able to initiate a trial and not make a response, but these ignored trials made up a small fraction of all trials and were not considered during our analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data shown in a figure.

claim: Throughout learning the individual did not follow the OPC.
source: Transforming this trajectory to speed-accuracy space revealed that throughout learning the individual did not follow the OPC (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The RNN performs an integration through time.
source: Here, the RNN already performs an integration through time (a choice motivated by prior experiments in rodents Brunton et al., 2013)
evidence: This describes a feature of the model motivated by prior work.

claim: Prioritizing learning speed can achieve higher cumulative reward than prioritizing instantaneous reward rate.
source: and that prioritizing learning speed can achieve higher cumulative reward than prioritizing instantaneous reward rate.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model simulations.

claim: The best DDM parameter fits of the rats' behavior allowed their thresholds to decrease throughout learning.
source: However, the best DDM parameter fits of the rats' behavior allowed their thresholds to decrease throughout learning, failing to support the constant threshold model (Figure 4—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the DDM to behavioral data shown in figure supplements.

claim: DDM fits to the rats showed an increase in drift rate throughout learning.
source: Consistent with substantial improvements in perceptual sensitivity through learning, DDM fits to the rats also showed an increase in drift rate throughout learning (Figure 4—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the DDM to behavioral data shown in figure supplements.

claim: Similar increases in drift rate have been observed as a universal feature of learning throughout numerous studies fitting learning data with the DDM.
source: Similar increases in drift rate have been observed as a universal feature of learning throughout numerous studies fitting learning data with the DDM (Ratcliff et al., 2006; Dutilh et al., 2009Petrov et al., 2011Balci et al., 2011b, Liu and Watanabe, 2012, Zhang and Rowe, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There was no difference in initial mean session accuracy between the two groups, followed by significantly higher accuracy in the slow group in subsequent sessions.
source: We found no difference in initial mean session accuracy between the two groups, followed by significantly higher accuracy in the slow group in subsequent sessions (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is a finding from the RT restriction experiment shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The slope of accuracy across sessions was significantly higher in the slow group.
source: The slope of accuracy across sessions was significantly higher in the slow group (Figure 5d, inset).
evidence: This is a finding from the RT restriction experiment shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The fast group had a positive slope and an accuracy above chance by the last session of the experiment, indicating this group learned.
source: Importantly, the fast group had a positive slope and an accuracy above chance by the last session of the experiment, indicating this group learned (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is a finding from the RT restriction experiment shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The slow group trended toward a higher cumulative reward by the end of the experiment.
source: Similarly, the slow group trended toward a higher cumulative reward by the end of the experiment (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is a finding from the RT restriction experiment shown in Figure 5g.

claim: The LDDM qualitatively replicates all of the behavioral findings from the RT restriction experiment.
source: The LDDM qualitatively replicates all of our behavioral findings (Figure 5h–k).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 5h-k.

claim: Rats with the visible stimuli qualitatively replicated the same trajectory in speed-accuracy space that was found when rats were trained for the first time.
source: We found that the rats with the visible stimuli qualitatively replicated the same trajectory in speed-accuracy space that we found when rats were trained for the first time (Figure 2b, Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a finding from the learnability experiment shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The best DDM fits for the visible stimuli were those that allowed both threshold and drift rate to vary with learning.
source: Indeed, the best DDM fits were those that allowed both threshold and drift rate to vary with learning, as was the case with the first stimuli the rats encountered, and in line with the LDDM (Figure 4—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the DDM to behavioral data shown in figure supplements.

claim: Rodents are capable of modulating their strategy depending on their learning prospects.
source: Hence, rodents are capable of modulating their strategy depending on their learning prospects.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the learnability experiment.

claim: DDM fits indicated a non-zero drift rate even in the absence of informative stimuli.
source: Although there is no informative signal in this task with transparent stimuli, the rats could still be using stimulus-independent signals, such as choice history or feedback, to drive heuristic strategies. Indeed, DDM fits indicated a non-zero drift rate even in the absence of informative stimuli (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the DDM to behavioral data shown in a figure supplement.

claim: Bias seemed to increase with transparent stimuli in the direction that each individual was already biased during visible stimuli.
source: In general, bias seemed to increase with transparent stimuli in the direction that each individual was already biased during visible stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from the PsyTrack analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Perseverance and win-stay/lose-switch seemed to increase and fluctuate more during transparent stimuli.
source: Perseverance and win-stay/lose-switch also seemed to increase and fluctuate more during transparent stimuli, suggesting a greater reliance on these heuristics now that the stimulus was uninformative (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the PsyTrack analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: The lack of learnability in the transparent stimuli led to a change in strategy that was distinct from that with learnable stimuli.
source: Despite the fact that the animals' still engaged these non-optimal heuristics, the lack of learnability in the transparent stimuli still led to a change in strategy that was distinct from that with learnable stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the learnability experiment and PsyTrack analysis.

claim: A slight mean post-error slowing effect of about 50 ms was found that was on average constant throughout learning.
source: Indeed, we found a slight mean post-error slowing effect of about 50 ms that was on average constant throughout learning, though it was highly variable across individuals (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the post-error slowing analysis shown in a figure supplement.

claim: All other threshold strategies considered fail to account for the totality of the results.
source: All other threshold strategies we considered fail to account for the totality of the results.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the model predictions to the experimental data.

claim: There was a correlation between initial mean ΔRT and initial ΔSNR across subjects viewing the visible stimuli.
source: Consistent with these findings, there was a correlation between initial mean ΔRT and initial ΔSNR across subjects viewing the visible stimuli, indicating the more an animal slowed down, the faster it learned (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is a finding from the learnability experiment shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The rats with the largest change in RT started with a lower but ended with a higher mean iRR, and collected more cumulative reward.
source: The rats with the largest change started with a lower but ended with a higher mean iRR, and collected more cumulative reward (Figure 7b and c).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7b and c.

claim: Rats adapted their decision strategy to improve learning speed and approximately maximize total reward.
source: Our theoretical and empirical results identify a trade-off between the need to learn rapidly and the need to accrue immediate reward in a perceptual decision making task. We find that rats adapt their decision strategy to improve learning speed and approximately maximize total reward, effectively navigating this trade-off over the total period of task engagement.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Rats responded slowly upon encountering novel stimuli, but only when there was a visual stimulus to learn from.
source: In our experiments, rats responded slowly upon encountering novel stimuli, but only when there was a visual stimulus to learn from.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the learnability experiment.

claim: Rats chose to respond more slowly in order to learn quickly, and only made the investment when learning was possible.
source: This result indicates that they chose to respond more slowly in order to learn quickly, and only made the investment when learning was possible.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from the learnability experiment.

claim: This behavior requires foregoing both a cognitively easier strategy and relinquishing a higher immediately available reward for several sessions spanning multiple days.
source: This behavior requires foregoing both a cognitively easier strategy – fast random choice – and relinquishing a higher immediately available reward for several sessions spanning multiple days.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: By imposing different response times in groups of animals, the theoretical prediction that slow responses lead to faster learning and greater total reward was empirically verified.
source: By imposing different response times in groups of animals, we empirically verified our theoretical prediction that slow responses lead to faster learning and greater total reward in our task.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the RT restriction experiment.

claim: Rats exhibit cognitive control of the learning process, that is, the ability to engage in goal-directed behavior that would otherwise conflict with default or more immediately rewarding responses.
source: These findings collectively show that rats exhibit cognitive control of the learning process, that is, the ability to engage in goal-directed behavior that would otherwise conflict with default or more immediately rewarding responses (Dixon et al., 2012, Shenhav et al., 2013; Shenhav et al., 2017, Cohen et al., 1990; Cohen and Egner, 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental findings supported by citations.
